data.name: Headquarters Visitor Center
data.description: The Headquarters Visitor Center is 1 mile (1.6 km) past the Summit District entrance gate. Inside, park staff can answer questions at the information desk. A small exhibit hall features displays on the park's natural and cultural history. Restrooms are accessible from the outside and open 24/7. Please check park alerts for information on closures.
data.audioDescription: A one-story, tan building situated next to the park road. The outside of the building displays a National Park Service Arrowhead and the words "Visitor Center." A garden of native trees and shrubs is planted along the sidewalk to the front doors. A lobby with glass windows has a bench and leads into a small exhibit hall. The exhibits feature Native Hawaiian cultural practices. There are accessibility options for the exhibits available at the front desk. To the right of the exhibits is the front desk, where park rangers supply maps and brochures. Copies of the main park brochure in Braille are available at the front desk to borrow. Behind the rangers at the desk is a large painting of the park's incredible biodiversity. Next to the information desk is the cash register for the partnering bookstore, Hawai'i Pacific Parks Association. The bookstore offers hiking and birding guides, books on Native Hawaiian history and culture, and educational children's books. Postcards, magnets, t-shirts, and a small selection of snacks are also available. By the windows looking out to the road is the Headquarters Visitor Center stamp on a small table. The stamp says "Haleakalā National Park, Headquarters" and shows the current date and a small engraving of a nēnē. There is green ink and sheets of paper available next to the stamp on the table. All throughout the visitor center are realistic models of some of Hawai'i's native birds perched on branches by the ceiling. The models feature the i'iwi, which is a bright red bird with a long, curved, red beak. There is also the 'apapane, which is red and white, and the 'alauahio and the 'amakihi, which are both yellow birds.

data.name: Haleakalā Visitor Center
data.description: About a 30 minute drive from the Headquarters Visitor Center, the Haleakalā Visitor Center is perched on the edge of the impressive volcanic valley. Inside, park staff can answer questions at the information desk. Visitors can learn about the history of the mountain through various displays. There is also a Hawaiʻi Pacific Parks Association bookstore with souvenirs available for purchase. Restrooms are located nearby in a separate building and are open 24/7. Please check the alerts page for any closures.
data.audioDescription: A four-step stairwell and paved path lead from the parking lot up to a small rock visitor center perched on the edge of the Haleakalā crater. A metal railing extends on one side with uneven gravel and rocky viewing area. A separate building with restrooms is along the paved pathway to the left out of the parking lot. The single story rock structure can be accessed by an entrance near the bathroom building or an entrance at the top of the stairway and paved path. Inside is a small bookstore with racks of clothing, books, and souvenirs in one area. There is an information desk and checkout area. Expansive glass windows provide views into the crater valley of the dozen cinder cones and valley floor several thousand feet below. There is a small office with closing door in the rear of the one-room visitor center space.

data.name: Kīpahulu Visitor Center
data.description: Located at the coastal Kīpahulu District. Information desk, exhibits on natural and cultural history, and a Hawaiʻi Pacific Parks Association bookstore inside. Restrooms are open 24 hours per day, 7 days per week, except when the park is closed during severe weather events. Please check park alerts for information on closures.
data.audioDescription: A one-story, tan building sits in a grassy lawn with native hala, or screwpine, trees casting shade to the right of the building. The outside of the building displays a National Park Service Arrowhead and the words "Visitor Center." A painting of the demigod Maui snaring the sun is next to the National Park Service arrowhead. To the left of the building is a deck with bunches overlooking the blue sea. On clear days, the island of Hawaiʻi can be seen in the distance with it's four peaks rising out of the ocean. In front of the building is a flagpole with the United States Flag and Hawaiian State Flag. A pathway leading off to the left guides visitors towards park trails and there are interpretive waysides along the path. Inside the building there are exhibits on Native Hawaiian cultural practices and Native Hawaiian history. A traditionally carved waʻa, or canoe, is positioned in the center of the exhibit area. To the right of the exhibits is the front desk, where park rangers supply maps and brochures. Next to the information desk is the cash register for the partnering bookstore, Hawai'i Pacific Parks Association. The bookstore offers hiking and birding guides, books on Native Hawaiian history and culture, and educational children's books. Postcards, magnets, t-shirts, and a small selection of snacks are also available. To the left of the cash register is the park stamp which says "Haleakalā National Park, Kīpahulu, HI" and shows the current date and a small engraving of kalo, or taro plant. There is green ink and sheets of paper available next to the stamp on the table. Hanging from the ceiling is a realistic model of the ʻiwa, or frigate bird, with deep black coloration, a forked tail, and a seven-foot wingspan.
